title: A song without words
hookLine: Hasidic prayer uses wordless melodies to lift the heart

lines: A TUNE HUMMED IN THE CAR.
A HUNDRED PEOPLE AT A TABLE.
cards: There's a tune you hum when nobody's listening. In the car. Doing dishes.
Rocking a baby at two in the morning. There are no words, or you've forgotten them, and it doesn't matter. The humming settles you.
Now picture a long table on a Friday night, a hundred people around it, and the rebbe at the head. Someone starts a slow melody. Yai, dai, dai.
Nobody sings a single word. And the whole room starts to rise.

teach.b: Niggun means melody, and Hasidism made it into something close to a form of prayer.
Many niggunim have no words at all, just sounds: yai-dai-dai, bim-bam, ai-ai-ai. Some are slow and aching, some fast and joyful, built for dancing.

Every Hasidic community has its own, passed down from rebbe to disciple, some for more than two hundred years. They're sung at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, before prayer, at weddings. Why no words?
A saying often attributed to Shneur Zalman of Liadi puts it this way: words are the pen of the heart, but melody is the pen of the soul. Words can only say what you already understand.
A melody can carry what you can't put into words: longing, grief, joy, a closeness to God that sentences would only shrink. There's a hint in the Bible, too.

When the prophet Elisha needed to prophesy, he said: "But now bring me a minstrel." As the musician played, the hand of the Lord came on him. In Hebrew, the word for playing there comes from the same root as niggun.
Music, in that story, opens a door. And a niggun has a shape: it often starts low and slow, repeats and repeats, climbs, then returns. That repetition is the point.
By the sixth or seventh time, you stop thinking about the tune. You're just inside it.
That's the lift Hasidim are after. Not performance. Not a good voice.
Just a heart carried upward on a sound.

how: Hasidic communities sing niggunim at the Shabbat table, at gatherings called farbrengens or tisches, before prayer and at weddings; many other Jewish communities have adopted them too.

games.q: the prophet Elisha is asked for a word from God, and he's troubled. what does he ask for?
games.why: he says: bring me a minstrel. as the music plays, the hand of the Lord comes upon him.

practice: Let a simple melody come, any melody, or make one up with three or four notes, and hum it quietly, or inside if you can't make sound.
Don't try to sing well; just repeat it, a little slower each time, until you stop thinking about the tune and rest inside it. If you pray, let the melody be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Niggun. A Hasidic melody, often with no words, sung over and over until the heart lifts. Words are the pen of the heart; melody, the pen of the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: a song with no words. Where words run out, a melody can still go. Until tomorrow.
